title: Spider mites in outdoor tomatoes - Tanzania

Header: Spider mites in outdoor tomatoes - Tanzania
Tetranychus spp. Utitiri wekundu in Swahili

Prevention: Use varieties that can tolerate some mites (e.g.
Do not place plots with young tomatoes next to plots with older tomatoes where mites can mass proliferate and migrate to younger plants.
Irrigate to strengthen plants and reduce impact of mites damage.
Note that moist conditions, particularly overhead irrigation, can promote certain diseases.
Remove and bury or burn all debris after harvest as mites can survive up to 6 months in debris, or move to adjacent younger tomatoes.
Monitoring: Spider mites are tiny, but can be seen with a hand lens.
They usually attack the undersides of the leaves, and cause tiny white yellowish spots on both leaf surfaces.
At heavy mite feeding, leaves become silvery.
Heavily infested leaves covered with fine webs, may turn yellow, and dry up.
Spider mites can occur any time in all stages of growth.
After first detection on several plants, one spray with a green direct control measures allowed.
When further infestations occur on 3 out of 10 plants, then consider further actions.
Direct Control: Neem extract. (2.5-3 litres/ha or 50-60 ml /20 litres water).
Or use 20-50g neem seed cake or seed powder / litre water.
Start 15 days after transplanting. 2% horticultural oil (1/3 cup oil in 4 litres water) at 6 week interval.
Garlic bulb oil spray (20 fine shopped garlic cloves soaked 1 day in 100ml mineral oil, then + 10ml soap, stir, add 2 litre water, stir) over plants max 2 times.
Strong water sprays drop mites to ground.
But this can promote certain diseases.
Restrictions: Only use pesticides that kill mites.
Search for the word acaricide (= mite pesticides).
Spray directly on underside of leaves.
In older plants, spray after staking and pruning to increase chance to hit mites.
When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label.
